title: Easement Appurtenant Foreclosure
subject: Real Property
subtopic: Appurtenant easement passes with dominant estate through foreclosure
stem: A recorded appurtenant easement granting the owner of Parcel A the right to cross Parcel B for ingress and egress was filed in the county records. Peter owned Parcel A, on which he operated a small tutoring academy. Peter later secured a business loan using Parcel A as collateral. The lender foreclosed on the loan, and Silas purchased Parcel A at the foreclosure sale. The foreclosure deed made no reference to the easement. Lydia, who owns Parcel B, contends that Silas acquired no easement rights. Who prevails?

choices.A: Lydia, because appurtenant easements transfer only through a voluntary warranty deed.
choices.B: Silas, but only if he proves strict necessity for crossing Parcel B.
choices.C: Silas, because an appurtenant easement generally passes with the dominant estate even when the foreclosure deed is silent on the point.
choices.D: Lydia, because a foreclosure sale never transfers appurtenant easements to the purchaser.

rightExplanation: An easement appurtenant is an interest in land that belongs to the dominant estate, not to the individual who holds it. When the dominant parcel changes hands — whether by warranty deed, quitclaim deed, or foreclosure sale — the appurtenant benefit transfers as an incident of the land. The foreclosure deed's silence does not extinguish the easement; it passes automatically because it was recorded and benefits Parcel A. Silas acquired Parcel A and all its appurtenant incidents. Lydia's parcel remains the servient estate. Silas prevails.

wrongExplanations.A: The type of deed used to convey the dominant estate is irrelevant to whether an appurtenant easement follows. Sheriff's deeds, quitclaim deeds, and foreclosure deeds carry appurtenant benefits just as warranty deeds do. The easement travels with Parcel A regardless of deed form.
wrongExplanations.B: Necessity is an element for implying an easement when no express easement exists. Here the easement is express and recorded. Silas need not prove strict necessity; the recorded right belongs to him as the owner of the dominant estate.
wrongExplanations.D: Foreclosure terminates interests that burdened the foreclosed estate, such as junior liens. It does not strip benefits that ran in favor of the estate. Appurtenant benefits survive a foreclosure of the dominant parcel and vest in the foreclosure buyer.
